question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

PERSPICACIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Discerning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Perspicacious (adjective) means having keen insight and sound judgement; quick to notice and understand what is not obvious. (सूक्ष्मदर्शी, तीक्ष्णबुद्धि)
◦ Example: A perspicacious reader will notice the contradiction in the second paragraph.

 

• Discerning carries the same sense — showing good judgement and the ability to see fine distinctions. (विवेकशील)
◦ Example: The award is given by a panel of discerning critics.

 

• The word comes from Latin perspicere, "to see through" — the same root as perspective and conspicuous.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Obtuse (मंदबुद्धि): slow to understand; dull of perception — the opposite of perspicacious.

 

• Option 2: Naive (भोला, अननुभवी): lacking experience or judgement — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Gullible (जो आसानी से ठगा जा सके): easily deceived or cheated — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of perspicacious: astute, shrewd, sagacious, percipient, judicious.

 

• Do not confuse it with perspicuous, which means clearly expressed and easy to understand — that describes the writing, not the reader.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

INDIGENOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Exotic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indigenous (adjective) means originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native to a region. (स्वदेशी, मूल निवासी)
◦ Example: The teak forests are indigenous to central India.

 

• Its true opposite is exotic — introduced from another country; foreign in origin. (विदेशी)
◦ Example: Several exotic species were planted in the botanical garden.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Native (देशी): belonging to a place by birth or origin — a direct synonym.

 

• Option 2: Aboriginal (आदिवासी): inhabiting a land from the earliest times — also a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Innate (जन्मजात): inborn or natural to a person's character. It is a near-synonym in the sense of "inherent", and refers to qualities rather than places.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of indigenous: foreign, alien, imported, non-native, introduced.

 

• In SSC antonym questions the setter usually supplies three synonyms and one antonym. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then discard every option that agrees with it.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To bell the cat
option_1: To warn others of an approaching danger
option_2: To undertake a dangerous task on behalf of everyone
option_3: To make a great deal of noise about nothing
option_4: To flatter a superior for personal gain
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To undertake a dangerous task on behalf of everyone.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To bell the cat" means to take on a risky or difficult task for the benefit of a group, especially one that everybody agrees is necessary but nobody is willing to attempt. (खतरनाक काम का बीड़ा उठाना)
◦ Example: Everyone wanted the decision reversed, but no one was ready to bell the cat before the committee.

 

• The idiom comes from Aesop's fable in which the mice agree that a bell round the cat's neck would warn them of its approach — until one asks who will actually put it there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes giving a warning, which is only the purpose of the bell, not the meaning of the idiom — the commonest trap in this question.

 

• Option 3 describes needless fuss, for which the idiom would be "to make a mountain out of a molehill".

 

• Option 4 describes flattery — nearer to "to curry favour" or "to butter someone up".

 

NOTE

 

• Other idioms of risk and initiative asked in SSC: "To take the bull by the horns" (to face a difficulty boldly), "To put one's neck on the line", "To go out on a limb" and "To bite the bullet".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

OBLOQUY
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Acclaim.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Obloquy (noun) means strong public criticism or verbal abuse, and also the disgrace that results from it. (निंदा, अपयश)
◦ Example: The officer resigned after weeks of public obloquy.

 

• Its true opposite is acclaim — enthusiastic public praise or approval. (प्रशंसा, सराहना)
◦ Example: Her first novel won critical acclaim across the country.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Censure (भर्त्सना): severe formal disapproval — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Vilification (बदनामी): abusive and defamatory speech — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Defamation (मानहानि): damaging someone's reputation by false statement — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of obloquy: eulogy, commendation, applause, plaudits, encomium.

 

• Useful pair to remember: encomium / panegyric (high praise) versus obloquy / castigation / opprobrium (harsh abuse). SSC often sets one against the other.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the blood disorder marked by an abnormally low platelet count.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Thrombocytopenia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Thrombocytopenia" is the medical term for a deficiency of platelets (thrombocytes) in the blood, a condition that causes easy bruising and prolonged bleeding. (रक्त में प्लेटलेट्स की कमी)
◦ Example: The patient was diagnosed with thrombocytopenia after routine blood tests.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: THROMBO (clot) + CYTO (cell) + PENIA (deficiency, poverty). Reading long medical terms root by root is the reliable method in spelling questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Thrombocitopenia" — incorrect; the root is "cyto" with a y, as in cytology and cytoplasm.

 

• Option 3: "Thromboctyopenia" — incorrect; the letters "y" and "t" have been interchanged.

 

• Option 4: "Thrombosytopenia" — incorrect; the root is spelt with "c", not "s".

 

NOTE

 

• The suffix "-penia" means deficiency (leucopenia — low white cells); "-osis" often marks an excess or abnormal condition (thrombocytosis — high platelets); "-aemia/-emia" refers to a condition of the blood (anaemia, leukaemia).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A person who cannot be corrected, improved or reformed'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Incorrigible.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Incorrigible (adjective) describes a person whose bad habits or behaviour cannot be corrected or reformed. (सुधार से परे, असाध्य)
◦ Example: The warden described him as an incorrigible offender.

 

• The word is built from in- (not) + corrigere (to correct) — the same root gives us correct, corrigendum (a thing to be corrected) and incorrigibility.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Intractable (हठीला, कठिन): hard to control or to deal with. It is used chiefly of problems and disputes, not of moral reform.

 

• Option 2: Irrevocable (अपरिवर्तनीय): that cannot be taken back or undone — used of decisions, orders and agreements.

 

• Option 4: Incontrovertible (निर्विवाद): that cannot be disputed or denied — used of evidence and facts.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes: Indelible (that cannot be erased), Illegible (that cannot be read), Inevitable (that cannot be avoided), Invincible (that cannot be defeated) and Inaudible (that cannot be heard).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

So compelling ___ the evidence that the defence withdrew its objection at once.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. was.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with "So + adjective", the clause undergoes inversion — the verb comes before the subject: So compelling was the evidence that …

 

• Even after inversion, the verb must agree with the real subject, which here is "the evidence". Evidence is an uncountable noun and always takes a singular verb, so are and were are ruled out.

 

• The tense is fixed by the second clause: "withdrew" is past, so the verb in the first clause must also be past. This leaves "was".

◦ Example: So heavy was the rain that the match had to be abandoned.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1 and 2 wrongly treat evidence as plural.

 

• Option 4: is — singular but present tense, which clashes with "withdrew".

 

NOTE

 

• Uncountable nouns that always take a singular verb in SSC papers: evidence, information, furniture, luggage, machinery, advice, news, poetry, scenery, equipment and stationery.

 

• Other structures that force inversion: sentences opening with Never, Seldom, Rarely, Hardly, Scarcely, No sooner, Not only, Little and Under no circumstances.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The revised edition is far ___ to the first in both accuracy and design.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. superior.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank is followed by the preposition "to". Only a Latin comparative can be used with to; ordinary English comparatives require "than".

 

• "Superior to" means better than and is the only option that fits the given structure.

◦ Example: This variety of seed is superior to the one used last season.

 

• Latin comparatives are never used with "than" and never take "more" before them. Writing more superior than is a double error frequently tested by SSC.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: better — requires than: far better than the first.

 

• Option 3: greater — also requires than.

 

• Option 4: finer — again requires than.

 

NOTE

 

• Latin comparatives that take "to": superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, posterior, anterior, prefer and preferable.

 

• Note also: prefer takes to, not than — I prefer coffee to tea; and preferable is never used with more.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The committee's report sought to ___ the rumours that had circulated since the audit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. dispel.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Dispel" means to drive away or cause to disappear — it is the standard verb used with abstract things such as rumours, doubts, fears, myths and suspicion. (दूर करना, मिटाना)
◦ Example: The minister's clarification dispelled the doubts about the deadline.

 

• The word is built from Latin dis- (apart) + pellere (to drive) — the same root as expel, repel and compel.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: disperse (तितर-बितर करना): to scatter physical things or crowds in different directions — the police dispersed the mob.

 

• Option 2: dismiss (खारिज करना): to reject an idea as unworthy of consideration, or to remove someone from a post. One dismisses a claim, but rumours are dispelled.

 

• Option 3: disband (भंग करना): to break up an organised group such as a team, band or regiment.

 

NOTE

 

• Learn these fixed collocations for SSC: dispel a doubt/rumour/myth; disperse a crowd; dissipate energy or a fortune; dissuade a person; defuse a tense situation.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The training programme aims at improving communication, (1)/ building confidence among the recruits (2)/ and to develop a sense of teamwork (3)/ before they are posted to the field. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of parallelism. Items joined in a series must all take the same grammatical form.

 

• The verb phrase is "aims at", and at is a preposition, so every item in the list must be a gerund (V-ing). The first two items follow this — improving, building — but the third switches to an infinitive, to develop.

◦ Corrected sentence: The training programme aims at improving communication, building confidence among the recruits and developing a sense of teamwork before they are posted to the field.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — aim at + gerund is the right structure, and improving is properly formed.

 

• Part (2) is correct — building keeps the series parallel.

 

• Part (4) is correct — before they are posted is a well-formed subordinate clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Parallelism is enforced most strictly after correlative conjunctions: not only … but also, either … or, neither … nor, both … and. Whatever form follows the first member must follow the second.

 

• Remember that at, in, on, of, for, from and the "to" of "look forward to" are prepositions, and every preposition takes a gerund, never an infinitive.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The witness told the court (1)/ that he has seen the accused (2)/ near the abandoned warehouse (3)/ on the night of the theft. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error lies in the sequence of tenses. When the reporting verb is in the past tense (told), the verb in the reported clause must also move into a past form.

 

• Since the seeing happened before the telling, the required form is the past perfect: "had seen", not the present perfect "has seen".

◦ Corrected sentence: The witness told the court that he had seen the accused near the abandoned warehouse on the night of the theft.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — "told" is rightly followed by a direct object (the court), unlike said, which needs to.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the prepositional phrase is properly formed.

 

• Part (4) is correct — "on" is the right preposition before a specific night or date.

 

NOTE

 

• Rule of the sequence of tenses: past reporting verb → past or past perfect in the reported clause.

 

• The one exception: a universal truth, habitual fact or scientific law stays in the present even after a past reporting verb — The teacher told us that water boils at 100°C.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

Why did the auditors ignore the discrepancies in the ledger?
option_1: Why were the discrepancies in the ledger ignored by the auditors?
option_2: Why did the discrepancies in the ledger be ignored by the auditors?
option_3: Why have the discrepancies in the ledger been ignored by the auditors?
option_4: Why are the discrepancies in the ledger being ignored by the auditors?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Why were the discrepancies in the ledger ignored by the auditors?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is an interrogative in the simple past, formed with the helping verb "did" + V1. In the passive, did disappears and the tense is carried by was/were + V3.

 

• The rule for Wh- questions in the passive is: Wh-word + auxiliary + object + V3 + by + subject?
◦ Active: Why did the auditors ignore the discrepancies?
◦ Passive: Why were the discrepancies ignored by the auditors?

 

• The auxiliary agrees with the new subject: "discrepancies" is plural, so "were" is used. The question mark is retained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps "did" along with the passive be ignored, which is ungrammatical — the tense marker cannot appear twice.

 

• Option 3 uses "have been ignored", the passive of the present perfect, changing the time of the action.

 

• Option 4 uses "are being ignored", the passive of the present continuous, which makes the action ongoing.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of questions: Do/Does + V1 → am/is/are + V3; Did + V1 → was/were + V3; Will + V1 → will be + V3; Has/Have + V3 → has/have been + V3. For Yes/No questions, the passive begins with the auxiliary: Was the letter posted by him?

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The old records cannot be removed from the archive without written permission.
option_1: The archive cannot remove the old records without written permission.
option_2: One cannot remove the old records from the archive without written permission.
option_3: One could not remove the old records from the archive without written permission.
option_4: Nobody can be removing the old records from the archive without written permission.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. One cannot remove the old records from the archive without written permission.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is a modal passive — structure: modal + be + V3 (cannot be removed). Its active counterpart is modal + V1 (cannot remove).

 

• The passive here is agentless — no by-phrase is given. When the doer is unknown or general, the active version supplies an indefinite subject such as one, we, people, somebody or nobody.

◦ Passive: The old records cannot be removed …
◦ Active: One cannot remove the old records …

 

• The modal "cannot" must be carried over unchanged, since it expresses the rule being stated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 invents an agent — it makes the archive the doer, which alters the meaning and also leaves from the archive redundant.

 

• Option 3 changes "cannot" to "could not", shifting the sentence into the past.

 

• Option 4 uses "can be removing", a continuous form that does not exist in this structure.

 

NOTE

 

• Modal passives to remember: can/could be + V3, may/might be + V3, must be + V3, should/ought to be + V3, have to be + V3. In every case the modal itself never changes form during conversion.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The office ran out of stationery a week before the audit.
option_1: The stationery cupboard was locked for the weekend.
option_2: She ordered stationery for the entire department.
option_3: The bus remained stationary for nearly twenty minutes.
option_4: Rising stationery costs were noted in the report.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The bus remained stationary for nearly twenty minutes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Stationery (with an e) is a noun meaning writing materials — paper, pens, envelopes and the like.
• Stationary (with an a) is an adjective meaning not moving; fixed in one place. The two are pronounced alike, so "stationary" is the homophone required here.

◦ Example: The train stood stationary at the outer signal for half an hour.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 all reuse the same spelling "stationery" in the same sense of writing materials, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: stationery contains e for envelope; stationary contains a for at rest.

 

• Other adjective/noun homophone pairs asked in SSC: complement/compliment, principal/principle, dependant/dependent, licence/license, practice/practise and prophecy/prophesy.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Every monsoon a city somewhere in the subcontinent is described in the newspapers as having been overwhelmed by an unprecedented downpour. The adjective is rarely justified. Rainfall records usually show that comparable quantities have fallen before, sometimes within living memory, without producing anything like the same devastation. What has changed is not the sky but the ground beneath it.

 

A city built on a floodplain is, by definition, built on land that a river periodically reclaims. For centuries settlements accommodated this arrangement: houses stood on higher ground, low-lying tracts were left as tanks, wetlands and grazing commons, and the water that arrived each year was allowed to spread, slow down and seep away. These were not empty spaces awaiting development. They were the drainage system, and they worked without pumps, budgets or maintenance contracts.

 

Their disappearance has been gradual enough to escape notice. A tank is encroached at its margins, then declared defunct, then filled and allotted; a stream is straightened into a concrete channel a fraction of its former width; a marsh becomes a bus depot. Each decision looks reasonable in isolation and is usually cleared on the ground that the land is lying idle. Only when the rain arrives does the cumulative effect become visible, and by then the water has nowhere to go but through the streets.

 

The remedy proposed after every such flood is almost always more concrete — deeper drains, higher embankments, larger pumping stations. These help at the margins, but they treat the symptom. Restoring even a portion of a city's lost water bodies would achieve more, and cost less, than any amount of engineering. The difficulty is not technical. It is that a wetland earns no revenue, while the plot that replaces it does.

 

Why does the author say that the word "unprecedented" is rarely justified?
option_1: Because newspapers exaggerate every natural event
option_2: Because comparable rainfall has occurred before without similar devastation
option_3: Because rainfall records are seldom maintained accurately
option_4: Because the monsoon has grown weaker over the decades
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because comparable rainfall has occurred before without similar devastation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The opening paragraph states it directly: rainfall records usually show that comparable quantities have fallen before, sometimes within living memory, without producing anything like the same devastation.

 

• The author then supplies the key sentence of the whole passage — what has changed is not the sky but the ground beneath it. The rainfall is not new; the city's ability to absorb it is what has been lost.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is too broad — the author questions one particular adjective, not the reliability of newspapers in general.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the passage, which relies on rainfall records as evidence.

 

• Option 4 is nowhere claimed; the author makes no argument about the strength of the monsoon.

 

NOTE

 

• When a question asks why the author says something, the answer is almost always in the sentence immediately following the statement quoted. Here the very next line supplies the reason.

What does the author mean by calling the tanks, wetlands and commons "the drainage system"?
option_1: They were built by engineers as an early form of sewerage
option_2: They were the only source of drinking water for the city
option_3: They were meant to be replaced by modern pipes and drains
option_4: They absorbed and slowed the floodwater naturally, without any machinery
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. They absorbed and slowed the floodwater naturally, without any machinery.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage explains that these low-lying tracts allowed the water arriving each year to spread, slow down and seep away, and adds that they worked without pumps, budgets or maintenance contracts.

 

• By calling them "the drainage system", the author is making a pointed argument: these were not empty spaces awaiting development but functioning infrastructure that happened to be natural rather than built.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 contradicts the author's point — the phrase without pumps, budgets or maintenance contracts stresses that these were not engineered works.

 

• Option 2 introduces drinking water, which the passage never discusses.

 

• Option 3 reverses the argument — the author regrets their replacement rather than recommending it.

 

NOTE

 

• When a familiar term is used in an unfamiliar way, the author is usually making a claim, not a description. Ask what the author gains by the word choice — here, the right to call the filling of a tank the dismantling of infrastructure.

Restoring even a portion of a city's lost water bodies would achieve more, and cost less, than any amount of engineering. The difficulty is not technical. It is that a wetland earns no revenue, while the plot that replaces it does.

 

On what ground, according to the passage, are such water bodies usually cleared for construction?
option_1: That the land is lying idle
option_2: That the water has become polluted beyond recovery
option_3: That the local residents have demanded it
option_4: That the courts have ordered their conversion
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. That the land is lying idle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph states that each such decision looks reasonable in isolation and is usually cleared on the ground that the land is lying idle.

 

• The author's argument is that the judgement of "idleness" is mistaken: the land was doing essential work, but work that produced no visible output until the rain arrived. The damage becomes apparent only as a cumulative effect, long after the individual approvals.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 mentions pollution, which the passage does not raise.

 

• Option 3 attributes the decisions to residents; the passage describes an administrative process of encroachment, declaration and allotment.

 

• Option 4 brings in court orders, which appear nowhere in the text.

 

NOTE

 

• Direct-detail questions reward precise reading. Note the exact sequence the author gives — encroached, declared defunct, filled, allotted — which itself shows how a water body is converted step by step.

Only when the rain arrives does the cumulative effect become visible, and by then the water has nowhere to go but through the streets.

 

The remedy proposed after every such flood is almost always more concrete — deeper drains, higher embankments, larger pumping stations. These help at the margins, but they treat the symptom. Restoring even a portion of a city's lost water bodies would achieve more, and cost less, than any amount of engineering. The difficulty is not technical. It is that a wetland earns no revenue, while the plot that replaces it does.

 

Why, according to the author, do engineering remedies fall short?
option_1: They are too expensive for most municipalities to afford
option_2: They require technical expertise that is not locally available
option_3: They treat the symptom instead of restoring the lost natural drainage
option_4: They take several decades to complete
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They treat the symptom instead of restoring the lost natural drainage.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last paragraph concedes that deeper drains, higher embankments and larger pumping stations help at the margins, but adds that they treat the symptom.

 

• The author's alternative follows immediately: restoring even a portion of a city's lost water bodies would achieve more, and cost less, than any amount of engineering.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 inverts the passage — the author says restoration would cost less, not that engineering is unaffordable.

 

• Option 2 is contradicted by the closing line: "The difficulty is not technical."

 

• Option 4 introduces a timeline that the passage never mentions.

 

NOTE

 

• The phrase "treat the symptom" is a standard signal of a cause-versus-effect argument. Whenever it appears, the author is about to name what he regards as the real cause.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Every monsoon a city somewhere in the subcontinent is described in the newspapers as having been overwhelmed by an unprecedented downpour. The adjective is rarely justified. Rainfall records usually show that comparable quantities have fallen before, sometimes within living memory, without producing anything like the same devastation. What has changed is not the sky but the ground beneath it.

 

A city built on a floodplain is, by definition, built on land that a river periodically reclaims. For centuries settlements accommodated this arrangement: houses stood on higher ground, low-lying tracts were left as tanks, wetlands and grazing commons, and the water that arrived each year was allowed to spread, slow down and seep away. These were not empty spaces awaiting development. They were the drainage system, and they worked without pumps, budgets or maintenance contracts.

 

Their disappearance has been gradual enough to escape notice. A tank is encroached at its margins, then declared defunct, then filled and allotted; a stream is straightened into a concrete channel a fraction of its former width; a marsh becomes a bus depot. Each decision looks reasonable in isolation and is usually cleared on the ground that the land is lying idle. Only when the rain arrives does the cumulative effect become visible, and by then the water has nowhere to go but through the streets.

 

The remedy proposed after every such flood is almost always more concrete — deeper drains, higher embankments, larger pumping stations. These help at the margins, but they treat the symptom. Restoring even a portion of a city's lost water bodies would achieve more, and cost less, than any amount of engineering. The difficulty is not technical. It is that a wetland earns no revenue, while the plot that replaces it does.

 

What does the author identify as the real obstacle to restoring a city's water bodies?
option_2: The absence of any workable engineering method
option_3: Public indifference to the annual floods
option_4: That a wetland earns no revenue while the plot replacing it does
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. That a wetland earns no revenue while the plot replacing it does.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage ends by stating the obstacle plainly: the difficulty is not technical — it is that a wetland earns no revenue, while the plot that replaces it does.

 

• The author is therefore locating the problem in incentives rather than in knowledge or capacity. A tank that prevents a flood produces nothing that appears in any account book; the building that replaces it produces both revenue and a visible asset.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1 and 2 are both ruled out by the sentence "The difficulty is not technical."

 

• Option 3 blames public indifference, whereas the author blames a financial calculation made by those who allot land.

 

NOTE

 

• In argumentative passages the final sentence usually carries the author's sharpest point. One question from every such passage is normally built on it, so it should be read twice.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The doctor suggested him to take complete rest for a fortnight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. suggested that he should take.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "suggest" is never followed by an object + infinitive. We cannot say suggested him to take. It takes either:

◦ a that-clause — suggested that he should take rest, or
◦ a gerund — suggested taking rest.

 

• Corrected sentence: The doctor suggested that he should take complete rest for a fortnight.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "suggested him taking" wrongly inserts an object before the gerund.

 

• Option 3: "suggested to him to take" corrects the preposition but keeps the impossible infinitive.

 

• Option 4: "suggested him to taking" mixes an infinitive with a gerund and is doubly wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs that do not take object + infinitive: suggest, propose, recommend, demand, insist, explain, describe, say. They take a that-clause instead.

 

• Verbs that do take object + infinitive: advise, allow, ask, tell, order, request, permit, persuade, warn, force. Compare: He advised me to rest (correct) with He suggested me to rest (wrong).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He has been working in this branch office since five years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. for five years.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The rule is fixed:

◦ "For" is used with a period or length of time — for five years, for two hours, for a long time.
◦ "Since" is used with a point of time at which the action began — since 2019, since Monday, since morning.

 

• "Five years" states a duration, not a starting point, so "for" is required.

◦ Corrected sentence: He has been working in this branch office for five years.
◦ Compare: He has been working in this branch office since 2021.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "from five years" — from needs a starting point and is normally paired with to or till (from Monday to Friday).

 

• Option 2: "since last five years" — a very common error; since still cannot take a duration, and adding last does not repair it.

 

• Option 3: "in five years" — in indicates the time within which something is completed (finished in five years), which changes the meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Since normally appears with the perfect tenses (has been, had been), while for may be used with almost any tense: He worked there for five years.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The teacher said, "The earth revolves round the sun."
option_1: The teacher said that the earth revolved round the sun.
option_2: The teacher said that the earth revolves round the sun.
option_3: The teacher said that the earth had revolved round the sun.
option_4: The teacher told that the earth revolves round the sun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The teacher said that the earth revolves round the sun.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Normally a past reporting verb forces the reported clause to shift into a past tense. There is, however, an important exception:

◦ If the reported clause states a universal truth, a scientific fact, a proverb or a habitual action, its tense does not change.

 

• That the earth revolves round the sun is a permanent scientific fact, so the present tense "revolves" is retained even after said.

◦ Example: He said that honesty is the best policy. / She said that the sun rises in the east.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 applies the ordinary backshift rule and so loses the universal-truth exception.

 

• Option 3 uses the past perfect, wrongly presenting a permanent fact as a completed past event.

 

• Option 4 uses "told" without an object. Told must be followed by the listener (told us that …), whereas said is used with that or with to + listener.

 

NOTE

 

• Other cases where the tense does not change in indirect speech: when the reporting verb is in the present or future (He says that he is busy), and when a historical fact with a date is reported (He said that India became independent in 1947).

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The old man prayed that God might bless the young couple.
option_1: "May God bless you!" said the old man.
option_2: "God may bless you," said the old man.
option_3: "God will bless you," the old man said.
option_4: "Let God bless you," said the old man.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "May God bless you!" said the old man.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "prayed … that … might" is the standard indirect form of an optative sentence — a sentence expressing a wish, prayer or blessing.

 

• Converting it back to direct speech requires the reverse of the usual rules:

◦ "might" → "may", and may is placed at the beginning of the sentence.
◦ The sentence ends with an exclamation mark.
◦ The third person "the young couple" → "you", the persons addressed.

 

• This gives: "May God bless you!" said the old man.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 places may after the subject, turning a blessing into a statement of mere possibility.

 

• Option 3 uses "will", which makes it a prediction rather than a prayer.

 

• Option 4 uses "Let", which forms an imperative of permission, not an optative wish.

 

NOTE

 

• Optative sentences in narration: the reporting verb becomes prayed, wished, blessed or cursed, that is added, and may → might.
◦ "May you live long!" he said → He wished that I might live long.
◦ "Would that I were young again!" → He wished that he had been young again.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The small brass band at the railway junction had not played together in nearly twenty years.

 

A. It had broken up when the mail train stopped halting there.

 

B. He traced seven of the original players, most of them now well past sixty.

 

C. A young clerk posted to the station found the instruments stacked in a locked store room.

 

D. They agreed to meet on Sunday mornings, at first only to see whether they still could.

 

S2. The junction now holds a concert every Republic Day, and the platform is packed by seven in the morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-C-B-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – C – B – D – S2. The paragraph follows a situation → cause → trigger → action → outcome order.

 

• S1 states the situation — the band has been silent for twenty years.

◦ A gives the reason: it broke up when the mail train stopped halting there. The pronoun "It" refers straight back to the band in S1, so A must come immediately after it.
◦ C supplies the trigger — the clerk's discovery of the instruments. It must precede B, because "He" in B can only be the clerk introduced here.
◦ B is his action — tracing seven of the original players.
◦ D follows B, since "They" refers to those seven players, and it leads naturally into the present-day scene in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-A-B-D) introduces the clerk before the reader is told why the band fell silent, breaking the link between S1 and A.

 

• Option 3 (A-B-C-D) lets "He" in B appear before the clerk has been mentioned at all.

 

• Option 4 (C-B-A-D) strands sentence A in the middle of the narrative, where the explanation is no longer needed.

 

NOTE

 

• The pronoun test settles most rearrangement questions. A pronoun — it, he, they, those — can never appear before the noun it stands for. Tracking It (A) → He (B) → They (D) fixes the whole order here.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The belief that lightning never strikes the same place twice is among the most durable of weather myths.

 

A. Tall isolated structures are in fact struck again and again, some of them many times in a single season.

 

B. A lightning channel forms wherever the path to the ground is shortest and least resistant.

 

C. The Empire State Building alone records more than twenty strikes in an average year.

 

D. That path does not alter merely because a discharge has already passed along it.

 

S2. The saying survives because it is comforting, not because it describes how the atmosphere actually behaves.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2. The paragraph moves from myth → principle → inference → general evidence → specific example → verdict.

 

• S1 states the myth that is about to be examined.

◦ B supplies the scientific principle — a lightning channel forms along the shortest, least resistant path.
◦ D must follow B, because "That path" refers directly to the path named in B. Together they explain why a repeat strike is entirely possible.
◦ A then gives the general evidence — tall structures are struck repeatedly.
◦ C narrows to a specific instance of A, the Empire State Building, and leads into the verdict in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-C-B-D) gives the evidence before the explanation, leaving "That path" in D with nothing to refer to at the end.

 

• Option 2 (D-B-A-C) opens with "That path" before any path has been mentioned.

 

• Option 3 (B-A-D-C) separates B from D, breaking the link between the path and That path.

 

NOTE

 

• Two reliable ordering principles appear here:
◦ A demonstrative such as that, this, such binds a sentence to the one immediately before it — so B–D must stay together.
◦ A general statement precedes a specific example, which places A before C.
